Photograph: Dave Decker/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Florida Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000 Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback calls failure to pay Briana Whatley money owed ‘an oversight’ Richard Luscombe in Miami Mon 3 Aug 2026 20.05 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 17.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded. Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse. A recording posted to Substack by Fishback in May 2024 shows Whatley, now a second-year history student at Florida State University, accepting a $10,000 check for besting seven other finalists in the 2024 Incubate Debate national championship, adding to two $500 area awards she previously won. According to Florida Politics , Whatley is suing Fishback for not delivering $8,000 of the money that a letter from the company promised would be paid to her in full on the day she graduated high school in May last year. The filing names Incubate Foundation Inc, the parent of Incubate Debate, and Fishback, 31, who is challenging front-running US congressman Byron Donalds and Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor of Florida, for the Republican nomination for state governor in November. The candidates face off in an 18 August primary. Whatley’s lawsuit, seen by the Guardian, was filed in small claims court in Broward county, where both she and Fishback went to school. Among the allegations are that Incubate Debate initially failed to respond to emails asking where the money was, then tried to change the terms of how it would be paid to her. Fishback, it said, “personally evaded and defrauded Plaintiff by initially ignoring communications, later blaming a terminated employee for the written award terms, falsely claiming an unwritten ‘installment policy,’ and delaying payment for months”. The document said Fishback admitted he “totally dropped the ball on this one” in a November 2025 text asking her to resend her bank details, then in December paid only $3,000 via Zelle. In another text, Fishback allegedly claimed that the employee who sent the original award letter promising payment in full on graduation had been fired, and that installment payments had “always been the case”, despite no previous mention of it. The text exchanges indicate a previously cordial relationship between the pair, with Fishback calling Whatley “a star”, and the student thanking him for “wanting to make it right”. Whatley claims Fishback broke off communication five months ago after she questioned why a promised 1 February installment was not paid. She is suing for the outstanding $8,000 plus interest and costs, and a pretrial conference is scheduled for 9 September. Whatley, the lawsuit said, has “suffered severe financial injury and out-of-pocket damages” as a result of Fishback’s alleged failure to pay. In a brief emailed statement to the Guardian on Monday, Fishback said: “This was an oversight on my part. We are fixing it.” In a court ruling last week, Fishback survived a legal challenge by Collins to remove him from this month’s primary. A judge in Tallahassee ruled that Fishback had not violated a rule requiring a gubernatorial candidate to be a resident of the state for seven years prior to the election, even though he bought a condo in Washington DC in 2020 that he declared his primary residence, and voted there. The lawsuit over scholarships follows a May 2023 episode in which Fishback and Whatley appeared to be on the same page in their criticism of the National Speech and Debate Association (NSDA), a rival to Incubate Debate, over censorship. Fishback wrote an essay for The Free Press , then owned by Bari Weiss, the CBS news editor-in-chief, stating that the NSDA had become a “woke” organization “hijacked by left-wing politics” that was telling students what they could and could not talk about. Whatley, then a high school sophomore, told Fox News Digital that she was warned by the organization to refrain from bringing up then former president Donald Trump during debates because it would be “inappropriate”. https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32418.text: When 193 nations gathered in Geneva this past July to debate the global governance of artificial intelligence, they produced a framework covering autonomous weapons, deepfakes targeting women, and the concentration of computing power in two countries — and said almost nothing about the algorithms now deciding who gets to vote. That omission may be the costliest blind spot in global AI governance, and two of the world's most senior election officials are now publicly demanding it be corrected before the UN reconvenes in New York in May 2027.Lisa Poggiali, the Chief AI Adviser at the International Foundation for Electoral Systems, and Samson Itodo, chairperson of the African Union Advisory Group on AI in Peace, Security and Governance, made that demand in an opinion piece published today by Rest of World. Their argument is not that deepfakes are irrelevant — it is that the governance community has confused the loudest risk for the largest one, and in doing so has left the foundational infrastructure of democracy outside the frame of any international accountability mechanism.Deepfakes Are Not the Threat to WatchThe 2024 global election cycle — sometimes called "the year of elections," when roughly half the world's population went to the polls — produced a clear verdict on the deepfake fear: the anticipated wave of AI-manipulated candidate videos did not measurably alter results. Fears that proved substantially overstated are now the primary frame for international AI governance as it applies to democracy — and that mismatch, Poggiali and Itodo argue, is a serious policy error documented by CDT.The deeper problem, they write, is structural: AI is being embedded in the foundational administrative machinery of elections themselves. Voter registers, biometric identification devices, identity databases, results-management software, and cloud infrastructure used by election commissions across Africa, Asia, and Latin America increasingly incorporate AI-enabled features — often supplied by private vendors operating beyond the reach of national electoral oversight. These are not systems that produce a fake video a voter can evaluate with their own eyes. They are systems that decide, silently and at scale, whether a voter's name appears on a list at all."Elections are not simply another sector affected by AI," the officials write in their op-ed. "They are the main mechanism that makes every other democratic right enforceable."India's Cautionary Case: Machine Learning and 5.5 Million Missing VotersThe clearest documented example of what administrative AI can do to an electorate comes from India. In March 2015, the country's Election Commission launched the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme, using a machine learning algorithm to cross-reference voters' photo ID records (EPIC) against Aadhaar — India's vast biometric national identity database of more than one billion enrolled individuals. The Wire India reports on the programme's design flaws in detail.The program had a structural problem that its designers appear not to have fully tested: the two databases were built on different data standards, different transliteration conventions for Indian names, and different biometric collection protocols. The algorithm flagged as duplicates or deceased voters records that did not match precisely — and recommended them for deletion. The results, when they became visible, were staggering: roughly 5.5 million voters were deleted from the electoral rolls of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana alone, many without any notice and with no clear path to reinstatement. India's Supreme Court halted the program through an interim order in August 2015.The accountability reckoning came through India's Right to Information mechanism — not from the election commission or the government. RTI disclosures revealed that the matching algorithm's failure rate had been as high as 93%, according to Poggiali and Itodo's account of the disclosed records. The figure deserves a moment of attention: a system failing nine out of ten times on the specific task it was built for — determining whether two database records describe the same person — operated on the electoral rolls of two Indian states before anyone outside the program had access to its error rate.The deeper governance concern embedded in the Aadhaar story is the one the authors call "a gradual transfer of electoral authority." Aadhaar is managed by the Unique Identification Authority of India, a statutory body under executive control — not a constitutionally independent institution like the Election Commission. Electoral data, in other words, flowed into a state-run system directly accessible to the executive branch, not to the institution constitutionally mandated to hold it.Despite the 2015 Supreme Court halt, the Indian government revived the Aadhaar-voter linkage program nationally through the Election Laws (Amendment) Act of 2021, extending the same structural risks — the same algorithmic design, the same data sovereignty questions, the same absence of independent oversight — to the entire Indian electorate.Are AI Chatbots Any Better for Election Advice?The administrative AI problem is compounded by a second, more visible failure: the chatbots that voters are increasingly consulting for election information are producing wrong answers at rates that should alarm regulators.During Scotland's May 2026 parliamentary election, the think tank Demos tested five AI services — ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Grok, and Replika — by putting 75 questions about three real Scottish constituencies to each service on a single day during the pre-election window. Across all five services, 34.1% of responses contained factual errors. ChatGPT produced errors in 46.2% of its responses. The errors were not marginal: the chatbots invented fictitious political scandals, gave the wrong date for election day, falsely told voters they needed ID at polling stations (they did not), and in at least one case fabricated a candidate who did not exist.These are not hypothetical errors about hypothetical voters. Demos polling in the week before the May 7 election found that one in five UK adults — approximately 10 million people — reported using an AI chatbot or AI-powered search service to find information about the local and devolved elections. Vijay Rangarajan, chief executive of the UK Electoral Commission, subsequently called for new legal controls over AI chatbot election information, while the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said defending elections was "an absolute priority" without committing to amending the Representation of the People Bill.During Hungary's April 2026 parliamentary election, researchers at the Civil Liberties Union for Europe (known as Liberties) tested ChatGPT and Gemini with voter profiles drawn from Voksmonitor, a respected Hungarian voting advice application, aligned to each of the five parties contesting the national lists. The results exposed a structural bias — not deliberate, but documented: ChatGPT failed to recommend the opposition Tisza Party in 90% of tests where it was presented with a detailed Tisza-aligned voter profile, and assigned Tisza a score of just 2% in percentage-based party matching tests. In 96% of responses from both ChatGPT and Gemini, the models recommended at least one party that was not on the 2026 ballot at all.Tisza won the election decisively regardless, ending Viktor Orbán's 16-year hold on power. But as the Liberties researchers noted, in a closer contest or among less certain voters, such outputs "could potentially impact the outcome." The regulatory gap they identified is real: neither the EU AI Act nor the Digital Services Act specifically covers AI chatbots providing voting advice, leaving them in an oversight vacuum.How Russian Operatives Are Poisoning What Chatbots KnowThe chatbot accuracy problem has a harder-edged dimension: state actors have identified AI information infrastructure as a vector for electoral influence and have already deployed it in real elections.The Center for Democracy and Technology, in a June 2026 analysis of the threat landscape ahead of the November 2026 US midterms, documented the emergence of "algorithmic poisoning" — a shift in influence operations away from producing fake content for human readers toward producing fake content specifically designed to be ingested by AI crawlers, so that the misinformation appears in AI-generated responses to voter queries. The CDT paper analyzes this as a systemic election security risk.The mechanism has two forms. In training-time poisoning, manipulated content is injected into the datasets AI models learn from — Anthropic's own research has found that as few as 250 malicious documents can introduce a backdoor vulnerability into a large language model, regardless of the model's overall size or the volume of its training data. In retrieval-time poisoning, bad actors flood the open web with coordinated content timed to be scraped by AI crawlers when users query the system in real time.The Pravda network — a Russian influence operation with no relation to the original Soviet newspaper — demonstrated retrieval-time poisoning at industrial scale, generating at least 3 million auto-generated articles in 2024 alone and distributing them across 150 websites in 46 languages, specifically designed to be indexed by AI crawlers rather than read by human users. A March 2025 audit by NewsGuard found that commercial AI chatbots directly cited Pravda articles as accurate sources.This operation was deployed ahead of Australia's May 2025 federal election, and a separate Russian operation called Portal Kombat deployed the same approach before Moldova's September 2025 parliamentary elections. The target is not a voter who sees a fake video — it is a voter who asks an AI assistant which party most closely matches their values, and receives an answer shaped by a coordinated information operation they will never see.What Did the UN's Geneva Dialogue Actually Decide?The inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance ran July 6-7 in Geneva, convening all 193 member states in the same room for the first time on AI. It was a historic moment in international governance, and TechTimes covered it in depth at the time.The Dialogue was not a regulatory assembly and produced no binding decisions — it concluded with a co-chair summary, in a structure deliberately modeled on the Internet Governance Forum. Its priorities, as shaped by Resolution A/RES/79/325, covered safe and trustworthy AI, capacity-building, the digital divide, human rights, and transparency. Elections were not a named thematic track.The UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, whose preliminary report was released to inform the Dialogue, mentioned AI and elections only in the context of disinformation and deepfakes targeting candidates. The report said nothing about voter register algorithms, biometric verification systems, or the accountability gap created when private vendors operate election infrastructure without being subject to electoral law.Poggiali and Itodo write that by leaving elections out of the AI governance agenda, the Geneva Dialogue "effectively removed the accountability mechanism for AI applications in every sector." The argument is not rhetorical: if you cannot remove a government through a free and fair election, you have no mechanism to hold it accountable for any other AI governance failure. Democratic accountability is the enforcement mechanism for every other right — and AI is now embedded in the system that administers it.The Accountability VacuumAt the core of the officials' argument is a question that global AI governance has not yet answered: who is accountable when a machine learning model affects a citizen's right to vote?In most jurisdictions, a voter deleted from an electoral roll by a flawed algorithm has no established legal right to receive the specific reason for deletion, no right to inspect the algorithm that flagged them, and often no clear legal entity against whom to bring a claim — because the algorithm was operated by a private vendor under a procurement contract, not by the election commission whose name appears on the legal mandate. The concept of administrative due process — the right to know why a government decision was made and to challenge it — has not been extended to algorithmic election decisions in most democratic legal systems. Poggiali and Itodo make this argument directly in their analysis."Absent clear governance standards," Poggiali and Itodo write, "election authorities may find themselves accountable for decisions embedded in technologies they did not design, cannot fully inspect, and often lack the authority to regulate."The opacity is compounded by scale. AI systems can process entire voter databases in minutes, flagging thousands of records for review or deletion before any human examines the outputs. By the time an error rate becomes visible through RTI disclosures or litigation, the affected voters may already have been unable to cast a ballot.Key structural questions go unanswered at the international level: Who controls electoral data once it enters a vendor's cloud infrastructure? Who has the legal standing to demand an audit of an AI system that flagged voters for removal? Who is liable when a machine learning failure affects the outcome of a race by suppressing votes in a specific constituency?Africa Is Building the Model the World NeedsThe authors point to the African Union as a concrete governance template that the international community has so far failed to replicate at scale.At its 1339th ministerial session on April 16, 2026, the AU Peace and Security Council adopted a communiqué affirming that Africa must "shape and control" its AI technology and ensure AI sovereignty across the continent. The Council's framing was direct: a corrupted voter register is not merely a rights violation, it is a trigger for conflict. That framing does two things the Geneva Dialogue's agenda did not: it treats elections specifically, not as a subcategory of "human rights" or "societal implications," and it grounds the governance requirement in regional political and security realities rather than abstract universal principles.Samson Itodo, who chairs the Advisory Group created by that AU Peace and Security communiqué, briefed the ministerial session on the specific conditions the AU has deemed nonnegotiable for any AI system deployed in electoral contexts: data localization (voter data must remain within national jurisdictions), technology transfer (election commissions must receive enough technical knowledge to audit what they procure), and disclosure of source code (the algorithm used to manage electoral rolls must be inspectable). These are requirements that address the structural accountability gap directly — they create the conditions under which an election commission can know what the AI system is doing and can contest its outputs.Lisa Poggiali has co-led the IFES AI AGE initiative — Advancing Governance for Elections with AI — since its launch in June 2025 at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The initiative's central premise is that electoral authorities and AI experts are "largely working in silos" and that elections cannot be made AI-safe until those silos are broken. Updates and resources from the initiative are available at the AI AGE updates page.How Does AI Know Which Party to Tell You to Vote For?The chatbot accuracy problem raises a question of mechanism that the Demos and Liberties studies do not fully resolve: is the bias in AI election advice a product of deliberate design, outdated training data, or something structural in how large language models assess political information?The Liberties research on Hungary found no evidence that the imbalance between ChatGPT's treatment of Fidesz and T

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-drops-sanctions.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5N4dU Alisher Usmanov (right) is a well known Russian oligarch with close ties to Vladirmir Putin Image: Alexei Nikolsky/Kremlin/REUTERS Advertisement The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman . It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved. "The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said. "The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added. Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years. Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom Image: imago/ITAR-TASS Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable." "Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. "Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media. Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list". Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs. France and Luxembourg sought exemptions France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list. Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details. According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov. Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg. Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions. Mikhail Fridman has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group Image: Mikhail Japaridze/TASS/imago images Who are Usamov and Friedman? Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin. The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators. For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank. Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions. https://www.dw.com/en/romanian-fighter-j.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OMmy F-16 fighter jets of the Romanian Air Force engaded drones over the country's territorial waters Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Romanian F-16 fighter jets have shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to the Romanian Defense Ministry. "Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea , moments after they had illegally entered our country," Defense Minister Radu Miruta wrote on Facebook. So far, no information has been released regarding the country of origin of the drones. What do we know about the incident? F-16 fighter jets shot down the drones some 20 kilometers (13 miles) southeast of Sulina. "The first drone entered national airspace at 17:59 (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes," Miruta said. He added that the second one was shot down at 6:05 p.m., five minutes after entering Romanian airspace. "The Black Sea will be safe again," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote on X. She added that NATO will discuss the issue at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday. Drone attacks endanger navigation in the Black Sea This drone incursion is the latest in a series of incidents believed to be a result of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In October, several drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea were reported off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. The most recent attack occurred on Thursday, when two chemical tankers were attacked off Romania's coast , leaving seven crew members missing. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal serves as an export route for Ukraine. Romania, an EU and NATO member, shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, part of which is along the Danube. The country has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania began shooting down these drones earlier this year.
